title: Sharp variance ordering for rotating Gaussian samplers
shortTitle: Rotation helps every observable exactly when friction is at least √2
oneLine: Rotation helps every observable exactly when friction is at least √2 — and what happens below it: for kinetic Langevin samplers of a Gaussian target, a target-preserving rotation never increases the long-run variance of any square-integrable position average if and only if the friction is at least √2.
abstract: A Markov chain sampler estimates an average from one long trajectory, and its accuracy is the long-run (asymptotic) variance of that time average. Adding a deterministic rotation that preserves the target (a nonreversible perturbation) is known to help every observable for overdamped Langevin samplers. For kinetic, or underdamped, Langevin samplers, which carry a momentum and a friction γ, Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis (2017) proved a local improvement for linear and quadratic observables of a Gaussian target when γ > √2 and conjectured it for every square-integrable observable. This candidate proves a global form of that conjecture: with matched position and momentum rotations, every square-integrable position observable has a long-run variance that never increases with rotation strength if and only if γ ≥ √2, the endpoint included. The mechanism is that the oscillator power spectrum is single-peaked exactly when there is no resonance, rotation shifts the spectrum, and convolution keeps single peaks single. The literal second-derivative form holds exactly on an explicit class containing all polynomials, while rough observables have sharper cusps. Below the threshold, even observables still improve at every rotation, only finitely many odd Hermite degrees can be hurt, and one finite rotation strength improves every observable. The paper also gives sharp large-rotation rates, a matrix criterion Γ³ − ΓK − KΓ ⪰ 0 for noncommuting stiffness and friction with least safe friction (2K)^{1/2}, a two-replica construction for arbitrary Gaussian targets, and shows that fixed horizons and regular sampling can reverse the ordering while Poisson sampling preserves it. Everything concerns exact stationary Gaussian dynamics; nothing is claimed about discretised integrators, cost or an optimal friction. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Sharp ordering (Theorem 1): for J ≠ 0, V_f(μ) is nonincreasing in |μ| for every real f ∈ L²(π) if and only if γ ≥ √2, the endpoint included; the decrease is strict unless f is rotation-invariant. This is a global form of the Duncan–Nüsken–Pavliotis conjecture.

Spectral criterion (Theorem 2): for any rotated stationary Gaussian process with integrable covariance, universal ordering holds iff the spectral density is nonincreasing on [0, ∞); for the kinetic oscillator S_γ(ξ) = 2γ/(ξ⁴ + (γ² − 2)ξ² + 1), single-peaked exactly when γ ≥ √2.

Below the threshold (Theorem 4A): for every γ > 0, even observables improve at every μ ≠ 0, only finitely many odd Hermite degrees can be hurt, and one finite amplitude improves every non-invariant observable; computed crossing points (Table 1) show only linear parts can be hurt for γ ≥ 1, and odd degrees up to 41 at γ = 0.1.

Regularity and rates (Theorem 5, Proposition 6, Theorem 8, Section 7): every variance curve is C¹, and C² iff Σ a_{n,ω} ω² n^{−3/2} < ∞ (a class containing all polynomials); polynomials converge at rate μ^{−4}, the worst case uniformly like √(2π/e)/(|μ|ω*), and more slowly or without any algebraic rate for incommensurate rotation speeds.

Matrix criterion (Theorem 10, Corollaries 11–12): for noncommuting stiffness K and friction Γ the ordering holds iff Γ³ − ΓK − KΓ ⪰ 0 (necessary for invertible J); the least admissible friction is (2K)^{1/2}, a safety boundary rather than an optimal friction; Γ² ⪰ 2K alone is not enough; two coupled replicas make the criterion apply to any Gaussian target.

Scope boundaries (Section 9): momentum observables, fixed finite horizons and regular sampling (aliasing) can reverse the ordering, while independent Poisson sampling preserves it. Results concern exact stationary Gaussian dynamics, not discretised integrators or computational cost.

narration: When does spinning a sampler make it more accurate? An Evidence Press briefing. Many simulations estimate an average by following one long random trajectory. Its accuracy depends on how strongly successive steps are correlated. A known trick is to add a gentle rotation that leaves the target distribution unchanged. For the simplest samplers, this is known to help every quantity being averaged. For kinetic samplers, which give the particle momentum and friction, the picture is different: in 2017 Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis showed that rotation can help, or hurt, depending on the friction, and conjectured that above a friction of root two it helps everything. This paper proves a global form of that conjecture for Gaussian targets. Rotation never increases the long-run variance of any square-integrable quantity, at any rotation strength, exactly when the friction is at least root two. The reason is simple to picture. The sampler behaves like a damped spring, and rotation shifts its frequency spectrum. If that spectrum has a single peak at zero, any shift lowers it, and combining spectra keeps a single peak single. Below root two the spring resonates, the spectrum has a hump, and a small rotation can land on it. Even then, the paper shows that symmetric quantities always improve, and that a large enough rotation improves everything. It also gives an exact matrix version, and shows that sampling at regular intervals can reverse the benefit. The limits matter: the results are exact for Gaussian targets in continuous time, and they say nothing about computational cost or step-size errors, and the threshold is a safety boundary, not a recommended friction. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate. Published on the fourth of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and code are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Duncan, Nüsken and Pavliotis (2017), Using Perturbed Underdamped Langevin Dynamics to Efficiently Sample from Probability Distributions. Journal of Statistical Physics 169. The originating paper: local improvement for linear and quadratic observables of a Gaussian target when γ > √2, the all-observable conjecture proved here in a global form, and small-friction numerics.
Nüsken (2018), Topics in sampling schemes based on Markov processes. Doctoral thesis, Imperial College London. Restates the conjecture (p. 62).

Hwang, Normand and Wu (2015), Variance reduction for diffusions. Stochastic Processes and their Applications 125. For overdamped samplers, nonreversible perturbations never increase the asymptotic variance.

Rey-Bellet and Spiliopoulos (2015), Irreversible Langevin samplers and variance reduction: a large deviations approach. Nonlinearity 28. Overdamped variance reduction, monotone in the perturbation strength.
Duncan, Lelièvre and Pavliotis (2016), Variance Reduction Using Nonreversible Langevin Samplers. Journal of Statistical Physics 163. Nonreversible overdamped samplers and their asymptotic variance.

Chak, Kantas, Lelièvre and Pavliotis (2023), Optimal friction matrix for underdamped Langevin sampling. ESAIM: Mathematical Modelling and Numerical Analysis 57. Optimises friction for a given observable, a different question from the safety threshold here.

Lelièvre, Nier and Pavliotis (2013), Optimal Non-reversible Linear Drift for the Convergence to Equilibrium of a Diffusion. Journal of Statistical Physics 152. Optimises the rate of convergence rather than variance ordering.

Breuer and Major (1983), Central limit theorems for non-linear functionals of Gaussian fields. Journal of Multivariate Analysis 13. Hermite covariance and spectral-convolution identities used here, credited.

Maini (2026), Spectral delocalization and central limit theorems for Fourier functionals of stationary Gaussian fields. arXiv:2610.37113. States the same convolution-power variance formula at a fixed frequency; credited, it does not treat monotonicity or samplers.

Lefèvre and Utev (2013), Convolution property and exponential bounds for symmetric monotone densities. ESAIM: Probability and Statistics 17. Closure of symmetric unimodality under convolution, credited.
Ohzeki and Ichiki (2015), Langevin dynamics neglecting detailed balance condition. Physical Review E 92. Replica duplication with nonreversible coupling, an established device used in Section 8.4.
Shapiro and Silverman (1960), Alias-Free Sampling of Random Noise. Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics 8. Classical alias-free Poisson sampling behind Section 9.4.
